questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Functions That Satisfy the Mean Value Theorem
questions.problem:
Which of the following functions satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[1,5]?$

- $f(x)={x}^{3}$
- $g(x)=|x|$
- $h(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function to satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[1,5],$ the function must be continuous on $[1,5]$ and differentiable on $(1,5).$

Let's check each function individually.

- The function $f(x)={x}^{3}$ is continuous and differentiable on $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ In particular, it  is continuous on $[1,5]$ and differentiable on $(1,5).$ Therefore, $f(x)$ satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $g(x)=|x|$ is continuous on $[1,5]$ and differentiable on $(1,5)$ because it is equivalent to $p(x)=x$ over the given interval. Therefore, $g(x)$ satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem. Note that the graph of $y=g(x)$ has a corner point at $x=0$ but this point does not lie inside $(1,5).$

- The function  $h(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x-1)$ is not defined at $x=1$, so it is not continuous at $x=1$, which means it is not continuous on $[1,5].$ Therefore, $h(x)$ does not satisfiy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

Therefore, only functions I and II satisfy the conditions for the mean value theorem over the interval $[1,5].$

questions.problem:
Which of the following functions satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[-4,4]?$

- $f(x)={e}^{{x}^{2}}$
- $g(x)={2}^{1/{x}^{2}}$
- $h(x)=\sqrt{x+4}$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function to satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[-4,4],$ the function must be continuous on $[-4,4]$ and differentiable on $(-4,4).$

Let's check each function individually.

- The function $f(x)={e}^{{x}^{2}}$ is continuous and differentiable on $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ In particular, it is continuous on $[-4,4]$ and differentiable on $(-4,4).$ Therefore, $f(x)$ satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $g(x)={2}^{1/{x}^{2}}$ is not defined at $x=0,$ hence, it is not continuous at 
$x=0,$ and so it is not continuous on $[-4,4].$ Therefore, $g(x)$ does not satisfiy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $h(x)=\sqrt{x+4}$ is continuous on $[-4,\infty )$ and differentiable on $(-4,\infty ).$ In particular, it is continuous on $[-4,4]$ and differentiable on $(-4,4).$ Therefore, $h(x)$ satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem.

Therefore, only the functions I and III satisfy the conditions for the mean value theorem over the interval $[-4,4].$

questions.problem: Which of the following functions satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[0,2]?$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function to satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[0,2],$ the function must be continuous on $[0,2]$ and differentiable on $(0,2).$

First, notice that the function $m(x)$ is continuous on $[0,2]$ and differentiable on $(0,2)$, so it satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem.

Let's check each of the other functions individually.

- The function $n(x)$  has a jump discontinuity at $x=0.$ Hence, it is not continuous on $[0,2].$ Therefore, $n(x)$ does not satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $l(x)$  has jump discontinuities at $x=0,2.$ Hence, it is not continuous on $[0,2].$ Therefore, $l(x)$ does not satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $p(x)$  has a jump discontinuity at $x=2.$ Hence, it is not continuous on $[0,2].$ Therefore, $p(x)$ does not satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $q(x)$  has removable discontinuities at $x=0,2.$ Hence, it is not continuous on $[0,2].$ Therefore, $q(x)$ does not satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Points That Satisfy the Mean Value Theorem
questions.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ is continuous on $[1,4]$ and differentiable on $(1,4),$ hence we can apply the mean value theorem. 

So, the mean value theorem states that there exists a $c\in (1,4)$ such that

$$
{f}^{′}(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.
$$

Plugging in $a=1$ and $b=4$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(c) & =\frac{f(4)-f(1)}{4-1} \\  & =\frac{2{log}_{2}⁡4-2{log}_{2}⁡1}{3} \\  & =\frac{4-0}{3} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{log}_{2}⁡x)=\frac{2}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{f}^{′}(c)=\frac{2}{c\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{c\operatorname{ln}⁡2} & =\frac{4}{3} \\ \frac{1}{c\operatorname{ln}⁡2} & =\frac{2}{3} \\ c\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & =\frac{3}{2} \\ c & =\frac{3}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Points That Satisfy the Mean Value Theorem
questions.worked_solution:
The function $f(x)$ is continuous on $[-1,1]$ and differentiable on $(-1,1),$ hence we can apply the mean value theorem.  

So, the mean value theorem states that there exists a $c\in (-1,1)$ such that

$$
{f}^{′}(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.
$$

Plugging in $a=-1$ and $b=1$ into the above gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(c) & =\frac{f(1)-f(-1)}{1-(-1)} \\  & =\frac{({1}^{4}-1)-((-1)^{4}-(-1))}{2} \\  & =\frac{0-2}{2} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{4}-x)=4{x}^{3}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{f}^{′}(c)=4{c}^{3}-1.
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4{c}^{3}-1 & =-1 \\ c & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
